title: Kirkland & Ellis to spend $500mn building its own AI technology
author: Suzi Ring · Kaye Wiggins

dom.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing by providing a concrete example of a major firm treating AI as a strategic operating and investment issue rather than a standalone productivity tool. Kirkland’s planned proprietary, partner-knowledge platform and willingness to reduce near-term partner distributions extend the synthesis on differentiation, workflow integration and protected investment capacity, although the platform’s performance and return remain unproven.

kp.k: Kirkland plans substantial proprietary AI investment
kp.d: The Financial Times reports on 28 May 2026 that Kirkland & Ellis has set aside $500mn for its own AI platform. Chair Jon Ballis says the firm expects to spend more than $100mn in 2026 and hundreds of millions more over the next three to four years developing custom AI services, in addition to continued spending on third-party AI licences. These are spending plans, not reported completed expenditure.

kp.k: Proprietary technology aims to differentiate institutional expertise
kp.d: Ballis presents the platform as a means of deploying the firm's collective intelligence throughout Kirkland rather than relying only on tools available to competitors. He argues that widely available AI raises the industry's baseline but does not provide the differentiation Kirkland seeks.

kp.k: Lawyers and technologists contribute to an exclusive platform
kp.d: According to Ballis, outside companies are building the technology alongside Kirkland engineers and data scientists, with 180 technology professionals working on it in total. Its design draws on information about working practices from 250 Kirkland lawyers, including 100 partners. Outside developers will not be able to sell it to others, and Kirkland will own, or have the right to own, all of it.

kp.k: Automation could accelerate outcome-based legal pricing
kp.d: The article suggests that automation of routine tasks previously charged to clients could overturn billable-hour pricing in favour of fees based on outcomes, described as value-based pricing. Ballis says Kirkland already uses value-based pricing on a number of matters and predicts that the trend will continue and accelerate, expressing the firm's intention to embrace it. The industry-wide shift is presented as a possibility rather than an established result.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article presents proprietary AI as a means of differentiating legal services and deploying institutional expertise, while predicting changes to pricing and documenting risks from misuse.
pts.d: Kirkland chair Jon Ballis says widely available AI raises the industry's baseline, but Kirkland seeks differentiation through a proprietary platform that distributes its lawyers' collective knowledge. He says the platform will support entire mandates rather than individual tasks, and that outside developers cannot sell it to others; Kirkland will own, or have the right to own, the technology. Ring and Wiggins report a $500mn allocation, additional to continued spending on third-party AI licences. They contrast this approach with industry purchases of Harvey and Legora tools and Freshfields' collaboration with Anthropic to develop tools potentially available to rivals. The authors suggest that automation of routine chargeable tasks could overturn hourly billing in favour of outcome-based fees. Ballis separately predicts acceleration of value-based pricing, which he says Kirkland already uses. The authors also report that financing the investment from revenue will reduce distributable equity-partner profits at least initially, and describe court incidents involving AI misuse.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Ballis's account of investment and implementation plans, reported commercial arrangements, and examples of court-related AI misuse—not measured performance results.
pts.d: Ballis is the source for Kirkland's planned spending, ownership arrangements, whole-mandate platform design and development inputs. He says 180 technology professionals are working on the platform, which draws on information about working practices from 250 Kirkland lawyers, including 100 partners. His pricing prediction rests on his stated experience that the firm already handles some matters using value-based pricing; no quantified pricing trend is supplied. The authors report Kirkland's prior-year revenue of $10.6bn as financial context, recurring industry deals with Harvey and Legora, and Freshfields' April Anthropic agreement. For misuse, they report Sullivan & Cromwell's admission to a US federal bankruptcy court that a major filing contained multiple AI hallucinations, and a London court's reprimand of Pinsent Masons for false AI-based submissions. These are individual incidents, not measured hallucination rates. The article supplies no benchmarks, productivity measurements or demonstrated performance outcomes for Kirkland's proposed platform, and its industry-wide billing transformation is framed as a possibility.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Investment is planned over 2026 and the following three to four years; implementation and pricing benefits remain prospective, with no specified date for a billing-model transformation.
pts.d: The article is dated 28 May 2026. Ballis expects spending above $100mn during 2026 and hundreds of millions more over the next three to four years, alongside ongoing third-party licence spending. Disclosure of the platform's name and participating technology companies is expected in the coming weeks, not necessarily launch or completion. The whole-mandate model is a stated intended use rather than an established result. Equity-partner profits are expected to be affected at least in the short term. Ballis predicts continued and accelerating adoption of value-based pricing without a numerical forecast or deadline. The authors condition the possible disruption of hourly billing on automation of routine tasks previously charged to clients. Freshfields' agreement and Sullivan & Cromwell's court admission are reported as occurring in April 2026; the Pinsent Masons reprimand occurred the week before publication.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are large law firms and their competitors, lawyers, equity partners, technology developers, clients and courts.
pts.d: Kirkland lawyers are intended to gain firm-wide access to institutional knowledge through a platform covering whole mandates, with partners contributing expertise to its design. Equity partners bear the near-term cost through reduced profits available for distribution. Rival firms would not be able to purchase Kirkland's proprietary technology from its external developers, whereas Freshfields' collaboration could produce tools sold to competitors and gives Freshfields early access to future Anthropic models and tools. Harvey and Legora appear as legal-AI software providers whose tools firms are adopting, not as alternative legal service providers delivering legal work. Clients could see a shift from payment for routine time-based tasks toward outcome-based fees; the article does not establish lower client prices. The reported hallucination and false-submission incidents affect the firms involved and the courts receiving their filings. No specific employment displacement or access-to-justice outcome is claimed.
